summary: Details a protocol to load Manufacturer Usage Description definitions from RFC 8520 for devices that do not have them built in, using QR codes. It is published to inform the community and as a base for further work. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Scan the code on a gadget to find out what it is allowed to do on your network.

subtitle: Scanning QR codes to tell networks what IoT devices can do

tldr.problem: IoT device manufacturers do not build in Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) support because networks do not implement it, and network operators do not implement it because few devices send MUD information. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9238 defines a protocol to encode MUD URLs in QR codes using the SQRL format. An administrator can scan a code on a device to obtain the URL pointing to a security profile, then configure network policies based on that profile.
tldr.outcome: Devices can communicate their network requirements via a physical sticker without requiring firmware modification, breaking the deployment impasse. However, this introduces social engineering risks and requires careful security practices around sticker authentication.

today: RFC 9238 is an Informational document published in May 2022 and remains current. It is not an IETF standard but serves as a reference for implementations. Adoption depends on manufacturers adding stickers and network operators implementing MUD processing, which has been limited. The approach remains practical for organizations with physical control over device deployment.

sections.title: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
sections.content:
RFC 8520 defines Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD): a way for a device to tell a network what kind of access it needs. For example, a smart lightbulb might say: I only need to talk to the vendor's server on port 443.

However, MUD never took off. Manufacturers did not add support because they believed no network devices would process MUD files. Network operators did not implement MUD processing because few devices sent MUD information. This created a deployment impasse.

MUD URLs can be communicated via DHCP, X.509 certificates, or the Link Local Discovery Protocol (LLDP). Each method requires firmware changes or special device configuration. Small IoT devices often lack LLDP entirely, and their DHCP clients are too restricted to add new options.

RFC 9238 breaks this impasse with a simpler approach: put the MUD URL in a QR code sticker affixed to the device. Anyone with physical access to the device can scan the code to obtain the URL. No firmware modification is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A device manufacturer does not want to spend money adding a feature to a device if nobody will use it. A network operator does not want to add code for a feature if devices do not have it. But if you can just put a sticker on a device and scan it with your phone, the problem goes away.

sections.title: How QR Codes Encode MUD Information
sections.content:
The RFC defines a format for encoding MUD information into QR codes using SQRL (Standardized Quick Response for Logistics), a data format developed for end-of-life device tracking. SQRL uses special control codes (record separators, field separators, unit separators) to structure data in a way that fits efficiently into QR codes.

A QR code starts with a header: [)> <RS> 06 <GS> 12N, which identifies it as a SQRL code. Then come data records, each consisting of a four-letter field identifier and the data value, terminated with a unit separator. The code ends with a record separator and end-of-transmission marker.

The RFC defines which data records to include: B000 (company name, mandatory), B001 (product name, optional), B002 (model number, mandatory), M180 (the MUD URL itself), and M06C (the device's MAC address).

The MUD URL should be as short as possible to keep the QR code small. URL shortening services can help, but must be stable for the lifetime of the device. The URL must not include a query string (anything after a ?); only the base URL is encoded.

The MAC address, if included, helps the network operator automatically associate the MUD policy with the specific device. However, including a MAC address means creating a unique sticker for each device, which is practical for manufacturers but not for third parties creating generic stickers.
sections.plainLanguage: A QR code is a small picture that encodes data. The RFC says what information to put in it: the company name, product name, model number, and the URL of the device's security profile.

sections.title: When and How to Use It
sections.content:
QR code stickers can be affixed by several parties: the manufacturer (best case, includes MAC address), an outsourced assembler, a reseller, a company importing the product, a network administrator preparing devices, or even a retailer adding value to the product.

The approach is most useful when an organization receives a large batch of new IoT devices and needs to configure security policies for them. An administrator scans each device's QR code, which provides the MUD URL and optionally the MAC address. The network controller then downloads the MUD file from that URL and applies the defined policies.

The MUD file itself is a JSON document that specifies which servers the device should be permitted to contact. Using MUD offers advantages over manually configuring access control lists: the policies can be updated centrally by changing the file, policies can refer to DNS names that map to multiple addresses, and the file can include additional metadata like a Software Bill of Materials.

The MUD file URL encoded in the QR code should be generic rather than firmware-specific, since a physical sticker cannot be changed if the firmware is updated. An operator should design the URL and file to only add new features over time, never removing them, to avoid creating security holes.
sections.plainLanguage: When a device arrives, an installer scans the QR code to get its network policy. The network then treats the device according to that policy: letting a printer talk to the print server, letting a thermostat call home, and blocking everything else.

sections.title: Security and Deception Risks
sections.content:
A QR code is just a passive label; it has no security on its own. The real risks come from what people might assume about the presence of a QR code.

False trust: The presence of a sticker with an official-looking QR code might convince a network operator or employee that a device is legitimate, when in fact an attacker simply affixed a fake sticker to a malicious device. Stickers are cheap and widely used; anyone could create a convincing-looking one.

MUD file authenticity: The network operator must verify the signature on the MUD file itself. Without proper signature validation, a network could be redirected to a fake MUD file with different policies. If using a Trust-On-First-Use (TOFU) approach to signatures, an attacker who intercepts the first request can substitute a malicious file.

URL shortening attacks: Short URLs are useful but risky. A shortening service could change its target, redirecting to different content. Using MUD file signatures mitigates this, but only if signatures are properly validated.

Sticker confusion: The wrong sticker could be applied to a device in error or via social engineering. An operator might scan what they think is the correct sticker, only to be applying a policy for a different device type.

MAC address leakage: If the QR code includes the device's MAC address, it reveals a device identifier. Such stickers should be placed on the device itself (ideally an inconspicuous part), not on the packaging or visible to security cameras. Machine vision systems might capture the QR code in photographs, allowing future tracking.

Privacy via URL shorteners: URL shortening services may track requests using short URLs, potentially allowing per-device or per-customer correlation of requests.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can print a fake sticker and convince people it is real. Someone can apply the wrong sticker by mistake. A shortened URL might change. The device's MAC address in the code could leak information.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 9238 is an Informational document published in May 2022 as an independent submission. Like RFC 9150, it is not an IETF standards track document and is published to inform the community and serve as a basis for future standards work.

The protocol is useful for solving the MUD deployment problem, but adoption depends on manufacturers adding stickers and network operators implementing MUD profile processing. At the time of publication, tools like MUDgee had generated MUD profiles for some consumer IoT devices, and research institutions had publicly released them.

The approach remains practical for organizations with physical control over device deployment, such as enterprises or service providers preparing devices before distribution. The social engineering risks documented in the security section require careful attention during any deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: This document explains how to use QR codes to tell networks about devices. It is not an official standard, but it is published to help people implement it correctly.
